task.title: Table of contents
task.shortdesc: A table of contents lists the headings of a document with the page where each one starts. CSSMedia builds it from the elements that you mark as headings, so the table is always up to date. The table of contents reference lists the properties, functions and at-rules that you use.

context.p: The element names in the examples, such as contents, chapter and title, are placeholders. Use the names that occur in your XML.

The table of contents and the bookmarks of the PDF come from the same marking. An element with a bookmark-level is a bookmark, and it is an entry in the table of contents. CSSMedia extensions have the prefix -cssmedia-, and CSSMedia ignores the same names without it.

info.p: Set bookmark-level on the elements that you want in the table. Level 1 is the top level. Elements without a level, which is the initial value none, are not listed:

The entry of an element has the text of the element. Use bookmark-label to change the text of the bookmark and of the entry. Its value is a list of strings, attr() values and content() values. The initial value is content(text).
A bookmark shows its child bookmarks when the PDF opens. Set bookmark-state: closed on a block-level element to hide them.
info.note: CSSMedia creates the bookmarks of the PDF automatically, one for each element that has a bookmark-level. PDF viewers, such as Adobe Acrobat, display them in a side panel. The bookmarks need only the bookmark-level declarations in your CSS. If no element has a bookmark-level, the PDF has no bookmarks. A table of contents is optional, and its options, such as -cssmedia-toc-depth and -cssmedia-toc-label, do not change the bookmarks.

info.p: Use -cssmedia-toc() as the value of content. The table appears where the content is generated. A pseudo-element of an empty element is a good place. The table can come before the headings that it lists:

Each entry is a block with the text of the heading, a leader and the page number of the heading. The entry is also a link to the heading. The table is empty, and CSSMedia leaves it out, when no element has a bookmark-level.
The table has no title unless you set -cssmedia-toc-title where content is -cssmedia-toc(). Its value is a list of strings, like the value of content:
The table lists every level. Set -cssmedia-toc-depth to the deepest level that you want:
The value all lists every level. The depth does not change the bookmarks of the PDF.

The title, the entries and the dividers have no element in your XML, so three at-rules style them. Each at-rule holds ordinary declarations, and its boxes inherit from the element that holds the table:

ul.li: @-cssmedia-toc-divider styles the dividers, which the next step explains.

info.p: Write a level after the name of @-cssmedia-toc-entry or @-cssmedia-toc-divider to style only that level. A rule for a level comes after the rules without level, so it wins. This example indents the entries of level 2:

The -cssmedia-toc-leader property sets the leader between the text and the page number. Set it in @-cssmedia-toc-entry. The values are dotted, which is the initial value, solid, space and a string. A string is repeated to fill the space:

step.cmd: Change the text of an entry

info.p: By default, an entry has the same text as the bookmark of its element. Set -cssmedia-toc-label on the heading element to give the entry another text. The value is a list, like the value of bookmark-label. This rule adds a word to the entries of the appendixes. The bookmarks do not change:
The initial value is auto, which uses bookmark-label.
A divider is a line of text before an entry. Use it to name a group of entries. Set -cssmedia-toc-divider on the heading element where the group starts:
The initial value is none, which adds no divider.

postreq.p: The same pattern gives page numbers in other places. target-counter() gives the value of a counter at the destination of a link, and leader() fills the space before it. The Links chapter explains how to set destinations with -cssmedia-link.
